description: Learn how to write your name in cursive: master the capital, the joins, double letters and hyphens, then practice with a tracing sheet until it flows.
excerpt: A step-by-step method for writing your name in cursive: break it into letters, learn the capital, plan the joins, handle double letters and hyphens, and practice from tracing to free writing.
lede: Your name in cursive is the word you will write by hand more than any other, and usually the first one you want to get right. Here is a method that works for any name, with three names written out stroke by stroke.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn to write your name in cursive?
faq.a: Most adults can write a short name neatly after four or five days of ten-minute sessions. A long first and last name with an awkward capital can take two weeks. Children usually need longer, and it helps to learn the lowercase letters in the name before the capital.

faq.q: Do all cursive capital letters connect to the next letter?
faq.a: No. In many school styles D, O, P, V and W end away from the baseline, so you lift the pen and start the next letter fresh. F, T and often Q and X are usually written without a join too. Capitals such as A, C, E, H, K, M, N, R and U normally connect.

faq.q: How do I write a hyphenated name or a name with an apostrophe in cursive?
faq.a: Treat each part as its own word. Finish the first part, lift the pen, add the hyphen or apostrophe, then start the next part with its capital. Dot i's, cross t's and add apostrophes after the whole word is finished, never in the middle of a join.

faq.q: Should I trace my name or copy it freehand?
faq.a: Trace first, then copy. Tracing teaches the path of each letter and join; copying next to a model shows whether you have learned it. Once you can trace your whole name neatly three times in a row, switch to blank ruled lines.

faq.q: Is my cursive name the same as my signature?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A written name should be readable letter by letter. A signature can be faster, looser and partly abbreviated, as long as you make it the same way every time. Learn the legible version first; a signature grows out of it.
